quote: **Every address that was discovered but not fetched is written down with its reason** — out of scope, excluded by the site, over the per-site cap, a failed fetch, or simply beyond the budget.
why: One category of discovered-but-unfetched address is silently dropped: the depth horizon. `apps/sigil/sigil/scrape/frontier.py:91-95` extracts every link on a fetched page (`page_links = extract.links(url, res.raw)`) but only enqueues them `if depth < self.max_depth`; nothing is appended to `self.skips` on that branch. The code says so itself in the comment two lines below the loop: "Depth-horizon links are simply never enqueued (bounded by design)." This is not marginal on the owner-facing path the same chapter describes: `apps/sigil/sigil/scrape/learn_source.py:34` sets `_MAX_DEPTH = 1`, so every link on every page fetched after the seed is discovered and dropped without a reason recorded. The sentence's own justification — "a silent cap would misrepresent coverage" — is exactly what the depth cap does.
fix: **Every address that was queued but not fetched is written down with its reason** — out of scope, excluded by the site, over the per-site cap, a failed fetch, or simply beyond the page budget. One category is bounded before it is ever queued and so is not itemised: links found on a page already at the depth limit are not followed and not listed. On the owner-facing "learn from this address" path the depth limit is one hop, so a reader should take the recorded skips as an account of the queue, not of every link seen.

why: The quoted sentence is seven words, not five: a / skill / is / guidance / it / authorises / nothing. quote:
registered. Three of the six have been proven against a real outside system: the two Kubernetes ones
against a **real Kubernetes cluster**, and exposed-secret validity against the **real GitHub
service**.
why: Chapter 1 contradicts its own census 980 lines earlier. §9.2 (line 105-107) reads: "Of the 38 kinds of checker, **3** have been run over material that a real outside system produced, **2** over material from real infrastructure the system creates and destroys itself" — and chapter 5's grade table names those buckets precisely: "**Outside system** | The procedure has judged bytes produced by a real third-party system on the public internet" versus "**Own infrastructure** | It has judged bytes produced by real infrastructure the system itself builds, uses and destroys" (05-weakness-types.md:1037-1038). Chapter 5's per-procedure table then grades `k8s_workload_posture` and `k8s_rbac_verb_grant` as "**Own infrastructure** — a real Kubernetes cluster the system creates and destroys" (05:1060-1061), NOT outside-system. The code agrees: tools/livefire/k8s_rbac_livefire.py:3 says the driver "creates a throwaway cluster we own", while tools/livefire/secret_github_livefire.py:5 drives "the real ``live_transport`` against the real ``api.github.com``". So of the six cloud/Kubernetes capabilities exactly ONE — exposed-secret validity — has judged bytes from a real third-party system; two more judged bytes from infrastructure VIGIL itself stood up. The same overclaim is repeated at 01:1070 (the §9.3 heading, "three proven against real outside systems"), 00-index.md:416, 04-leads-and-facts.md:1402 and :1534, 09-the-screens.md:1780, 10-the-picture-of-the-attack.md:705. Chapter 2 (02-the-parts.md:1476) and chapter 8 (08:2153) get it right, saying "fired at real infrastructure" / "fired at something real" — which is what makes this a live contradiction rather than a house convention.
fix: registered. Three of the six have now been fired at something real, and the three are not of equal weight: the two Kubernetes ones against a **real Kubernetes cluster the system stands up, owns and destroys itself** — own infrastructure, not a third-party estate — and exposed-secret validity against the **real GitHub service**, which is the only one of the six to have judged bytes from a real outside system.

quote:
Three are proven against a real outside system — the two container-platform
(Kubernetes) ones against a real cluster the system stands up itself, and the GitHub half of
exposed-secret validity against the real GitHub service.
why: Same defect as above, in the master index — the first page a government reader reads, and the page that carries the four-tier census. Twelve lines is all that separates the index's own honest four-bucket count (00-index.md:459 onward and the verification table at :715-719) from this sentence. The index's own summary at 00-index.md:104-110 uses the split correctly ("**3** have judged material a real outside system produced, **2** material from real infrastructure the system creates and destroys itself"), and it names the outside-system three as two general-purpose web checkers plus the exposed-secret checker (01-what-this-is.md:1036-1038) — the Kubernetes pair is not among them. The sentence quoted here silently promotes a self-built k3s cluster to "a real outside system", which is exactly the grade inflation chapter 5 built the four-grade ladder to prevent. Checked: `docs/capability-matrix/evidence-branches.json` registers the k8s live-capture branches, and `tools/livefire/k8s_rbac_livefire.sh` is driven by a script the repo ships to build the cluster locally — no third party is involved.
fix: Three have been fired at something real, and the index states which kind: the two container-platform (Kubernetes) ones against a real cluster the system stands up, owns and destroys itself (own infrastructure), and the GitHub half of exposed-secret validity against the real GitHub service — the only outside-system grade among the six.

quote:
If the question asked is instead "how many have ever judged bytes from a real network
connection of any kind", the answer is 15 — the thirteen local ones plus response differencing and
achieved state, which were exercised locally as well as externally.
why: The answer to the question as asked is 18, not 15. The sentence adds the 13 "real local process" procedures to only two of the three outside-system ones, and silently drops three procedures that demonstrably judged bytes off a real network connection: `secret_credential_validity` (graded four lines above as "**Outside system** — the real code-hosting provider"; `tools/livefire/secret_github_livefire.py:5` drives "the real ``live_transport`` against the real ``api.github.com``", an HTTPS round trip), and `k8s_workload_posture` + `k8s_rbac_verb_grant`, which the same table grades "**Own infrastructure** — a real Kubernetes cluster" and which reach that cluster over its real API server (`tools/livefire/k8s_rbac_livefire.py:4` — "captures what the real API server returns"). 13 + 3 + 2 = 18. Undercounting here is a defect in the same direction the chapter warns against in reverse: a reader who checks and finds three more network-exercised procedures than the chapter admits will trust the other counts less.
fix: If the question asked is instead "how many have ever judged bytes from a real network connection of any kind", the answer is 18 — the thirteen local ones, plus response differencing and achieved state (exercised locally as well as externally), plus exposed-secret validity over the real GitHub API and the two Kubernetes ones over a real cluster's API server.

Line 522 reads: "nine assistants in the mesh, plus a perception assistant: ten named identities that can write to the owner's record", and line 517 says the tenth "is built on the same foundation as the other nine — the same base class, the same routing through the governor, the same outcome written to the same record — and declares its own name and its own ceiling of A1". Chapter 14 agrees (14-the-sovereign-side.md:679, "The count: ten named identities, of which chapter 11 covers nine"). quote:
Within those families the coverage includes database-engine-specific variants for five major database
products, eleven distinct page-template engines, both Windows and Unix command variants, obfuscated
forms of the widely exploited Java logging vulnerability, and twenty framework-exposure paths
why: Ten template engines, not eleven. `engine/crucible/framework/v2/scanner/library_entries/` holds 11 entries with `bug_class: ssti`, but only ten name an engine — `m2-ssti-erb`, `-freemarker`, `-jinja2`, `-mako`, `-pug`, `-razor`, `-smarty`, `-thymeleaf`, `-twig`, `-velocity`. The eleventh is `m2-ssti-generic`, whose payload is the engine-agnostic `${31337*31337}` and whose gating condition is literally `"applies_when": {"always": true}` — it is a catch-all, not a distinct engine. The two neighbouring figures in the same sentence do check out: five database products (mssql, mysql, oracle, pg, sqlite across the 48 sqli-family entries) and twenty `exposure` entries. So does the table's 172 total — I summed the per-class counts from the JSON and every one of the 23 rows matches.
fix: Within those families the coverage includes database-engine-specific variants for five major database products, ten distinct page-template engines plus one engine-agnostic form, both Windows and Unix command variants, obfuscated forms of the widely exploited Java logging vulnerability, and twenty framework-exposure paths
